entry.name: Fired brick
entry.desc: Fired brick is brick of clay and shale baked in a kiln, harder and longer-lasting than the older sun-dried mudbrick. Mesopotamia had discovered it between 5000 and 4500 BCE, and the earliest fired bricks of China appeared around 4400 BCE at Chengtoushan, a walled settlement of the Daxi culture, where they paved house floors. Indus Valley cities such as Kalibangan used it by 3000 BCE, and the Roman legions stamped the bricks of their mobile kilns across the empire. The first brick-making machine was patented in 1852, as the Industrial Revolution multiplied production.

row.label: Fired brick
row.contested: Fired bricks are also said to have been used only since c. 4000 BCE. In China proper brick construction of walls and vaults emerged only in the third century BCE.

entry.name: Flying buttress
entry.desc: A flying buttress is a ramping arch that carries the outward thrust of a stone vault or roof from the upper part of a wall across open space to a massive pier standing away from it. Ancient examples survive on the Basilica of San Vitale in Ravenna and the Rotunda of Galerius in Thessaloniki, and Romanesque churches such as Durham Cathedral hid similar arches under their gallery roofs. By the 1160s builders in the Île-de-France ran longer, visible arches over the aisles, as at Saint-Germain-des-Prés, completed in 1163, and Notre Dame de Paris in 1180. Walls could then be thinner, with larger windows of stained glass, and the flying buttress became a defining feature of Gothic architecture.

row.label: Flying buttress
row.contested: The flying buttress was first developed in late antiquity: early, undated examples stand on the Basilica of San Vitale in Ravenna and the Rotunda of Galerius in Thessaloniki.

entry.name: Reinforced concrete
entry.desc: Reinforced concrete is concrete with embedded iron or steel bars or mesh, which take the tension plain concrete cannot bear while the concrete resists compression. It was developed in parallel in England and France in the mid-19th century. The French builder François Coignet built the first iron-reinforced concrete structure, a four-story house in the suburbs of Paris, in 1853–55, and in 1854 the English builder William B. Wilkinson reinforced the roof and floors of a house with knowledge of tensile stresses. Joseph Monier patented reinforced flowerpots in 1867 and columns and girders in 1877, and the firm Wayss & Freytag made the first commercial use of it in 1884.

row.label: Reinforced concrete
row.contested: Coignet seems to have used the iron to keep monolithic walls from overturning rather than to add strength; Wilkinson’s reinforcement of 1854 shows knowledge of tensile stresses.

entry.name: Portland cement
entry.desc: Portland cement is a hydraulic cement made by heating limestone and clay minerals in a kiln to form clinker, then grinding it with a little gypsum; it is the most common cement and the basic ingredient of concrete and mortar. Joseph Aspdin patented it in England in 1824 and named it after Portland stone, quarried on the Isle of Portland in Dorset. It grew out of the natural cements made in Britain from the middle of the 18th century, John Smeaton’s experiments of 1756 and Louis Vicat’s artificial hydraulic lime. His son William Aspdin improved it in the 1840s at Rotherhithe, and the rotary kiln, patented in 1885, allowed continuous manufacture.

row.label: Portland cement
row.contested: The name Portland cement was recorded in a directory of 1823 with a William Lockwood. Aspdin’s cement has been called a proto-Portland cement: his son William is regarded as the inventor of the modern form, and Isaac Charles Johnson claimed to be its real father.

entry.name: Hypocaust
entry.desc: A hypocaust is a system of central heating in which hot air and smoke from a furnace circulate beneath a floor raised on stacks of tiles, the pilae, and rise through clay or tile flues in the walls. Vitruvius attributes its invention to Sergius Orata around 80 BCE, and described its construction in his De architectura of about 15 BCE. Hypocausts heated public baths and the villas of the wealthy throughout the Roman Empire, and their remains survive across Europe, western Asia and northern Africa. The system fell out of use in the western provinces as the empire declined, but lived on in the Eastern Roman Empire and in the baths of Al Andalus.

row.label: Hypocaust
row.contested: The earliest reference suggests that the Temple of Ephesus was heated in this way in 350 BCE, and Garrett G. Fagan has disputed Orata’s priority.

The article is about the modern separate sewer for sewage alone and names no early sewer system and no date: its history says only that sanitary sewers evolved from combined sewers and spread from the mid-20th century.

entry.name: Vulcanization
entry.desc: Vulcanization is the hardening of rubber, originally of natural rubber treated with sulfur and heat, which forms cross-links between its polymer chains and makes it firmer and more durable. Ancient Mesoamerican cultures already cured rubber with sulfur-rich plant juices, an early form of the process. Charles Goodyear, who worked in the 1830s to strengthen rubber, found in 1839 that a mixture of rubber and sulfur dropped on a hot pan hardened instead of melting, and by 1844 he had patented the process and produced the rubber on an industrial scale. Thomas Hancock had taken out a British patent eight weeks earlier, in November 1843.

row.label: Vulcanization
row.contested: Thomas Hancock took out a British patent for vulcanization with sulfur on 21 November 1843, eight weeks before Goodyear’s US patent of 30 January 1844; accounts differ on whether Hancock had studied samples of Goodyear’s rubber.

entry.name: Friction match
entry.desc: A friction match is a small stick tipped with a mixture that ignites when struck against a rough surface. Pinewood sticks tipped with sulfur, lit from a flame, are described in China around 950, and in 1805 Jean Chancel of Paris made a match lit by dipping it in sulfuric acid. The first commercially successful friction match was made by John Walker, a chemist and pharmacist of Stockton-on-Tees, England, and first recorded in April 1827: sticks tipped with antimony trisulfide and potassium chlorate. Samuel Jones sold an improved version as the lucifer, and Gustaf Erik Pasch’s striking surface of red phosphorus of 1844 led to the safety match.

row.label: Friction match
row.contested: Walker may have made his first friction matches during experiments in 1826. Earlier French friction lighters, Cagniard de la Tour’s phosphorus bottle of 1810 and François Derosne’s briquet phosphorique of 1816, proved inconvenient and unsafe.

skip: The article gives no date for the first faience: the earliest evidence it names is faience beads in Predynastic graves at Naqada, Badar, el-Amrah and other sites, without a year, and no workshop has been confirmed.

entry.name: Egyptian blue
entry.desc: Egyptian blue, a calcium copper silicate, is a pigment made by heating silica, lime, a copper compound and an alkali, and is considered the first synthetic pigment. The earliest evidence of its use is on an alabaster bowl of the late pre-dynastic period, Naqada III, about 3250 BCE, excavated at Hierakonpolis. Egyptians made it to imitate turquoise and lapis lazuli and painted it on tombs, wall paintings, furnishings and statues; it is also found in the Near East, the Eastern Mediterranean and the Roman Empire. Vitruvius described how it was made in the first century BCE, but its use died out in the fourth century CE and the method was forgotten until modern analysis.

row.label: Egyptian blue
row.contested: The pigment is also said to have been first synthesised in the Fourth Dynasty. Whether its presence beyond Egypt reflects its spread or parallel invention is unclear.

entry.name: Lacquerware
entry.desc: Lacquerware consists of objects coated with lacquer, in East Asia an urushiol-based lacquer from the dried sap of the lacquer tree, Toxicodendron vernicifluum. The oldest known lacquerware, burial ornaments from an Initial Jōmon pit grave at the Kakinoshima site in Hakodate, Hokkaido, Japan, is about 9,000 years old, and the earliest in China is a red wooden bowl from a Hemudu culture site in Zhejiang. Chinese lacquer became a decorative art under the Shang dynasty and a commercial industry in the state of Chu under the Eastern Zhou, and spread to Korea and Japan; the traditions of Southeast Asia, South Asia and the Americas arose independently.

row.label: Lacquerware
row.contested: The Kakinoshima pieces are also dated to the 9th millennium BCE, and a lacquer tree of the Jōmon period is 12,600 years old. Experts are divided on whether Jōmon lacquer was invented independently or derived from Chinese techniques.

entry.name: Sulfuric acid
entry.desc: Sulfuric acid, called oil of vitriol by medieval alchemists, is a strong acid first made by distilling vitriols, the hydrated sulfates of metals. The Jabirian authors and Abu Bakr al-Razi distilled vitriols, and al-Razi may have made the acid unknowingly; according to Ahmad Y. al-Hassan, an anonymous Garshuni manuscript from before c. 1100 holds three recipes for it. European works first allude to it in the thirteenth century. Joshua Ward of London began large-scale production in 1736, John Roebuck’s lead chamber process of 1746 in Birmingham industrialised it, and Peregrine Phillips patented the contact process in 1831, by which nearly all of it is made today.

row.label: Sulfuric acid
row.contested: Al-Razi may have made it without knowing in a recipe of his Book of Secrets. An Arabic treatise with a recipe for it, falsely attributed to Ja'far al-Sadiq, is dated to the thirteenth century by Julius Ruska but earlier by al-Hassan.

entry.name: Electrolysis
entry.desc: Electrolysis is the use of a direct electric current to drive a chemical reaction that would not otherwise occur, as in separating elements from ores and compounds. In 1800 William Nicholson and Anthony Carlisle, furthering Volta’s experiments, placed the wires of a voltaic pile in water and saw hydrogen and oxygen bubble from them. Humphry Davy discovered potassium, sodium, barium, calcium and magnesium by electrolysis by 1808, and his assistant Michael Faraday published two laws of electrolysis and introduced the word in 1834. The method later yielded gallium in 1875, fluorine in 1886 and, through the Hall–Héroult process of the same year, aluminium.

row.label: Electrolysis
row.contested: In 1785 Martinus van Marum reduced tin, zinc and antimony from their salts with an electrostatic generator without knowing the process, and in 1789 Adriaan Paets van Troostwijk and Jan Rudolph Deiman split small amounts of water; Johann Ritter also demonstrated it in 1800.

entry.name: Hall–Héroult process
entry.desc: The Hall–Héroult process is the major industrial process for smelting aluminium: alumina, obtained most often from bauxite, is dissolved in molten cryolite and the bath is electrolysed at 940–980 °C, giving metal of 99.5–99.8% purity. It was discovered independently and almost simultaneously in 1886 by the American chemist Charles Martin Hall and the Frenchman Paul Héroult, both 22 years old. Before it, aluminium was made with sodium or potassium and cost more than gold; Hall opened the first large-scale plant in Pittsburgh in 1888, later Alcoa, and with cheaper electric power the metal became an inexpensive commodity. The process uses much electricity and can emit much carbon dioxide.

row.label: Hall–Héroult process
row.contested: Some authors claim that Hall was assisted by his sister Julia Brainerd Hall, but the extent of her part has been disputed.
